title: Book Five (1806 - 07) — Chapter 20
paragraphs: Rostov had come to Tilsit on the worst possible day for delivering a petition on Denisov's behalf. He couldn't go to the general himself, being in civilian clothes and having come to Tilsit without permission; and Boris, even had he wanted to, couldn't have done anything the following day either. On that day — June 27 — the peace preliminaries were signed. The Emperors exchanged decorations: Alexander received the Cross of the Legion of Honor and Napoleon the Order of Saint Andrew of the First Degree. A dinner had been arranged for that evening, given by a battalion of the French Guards for the Preobrazhensky battalion. The Emperors were to attend.

Rostov felt so ill at ease with Boris that when Boris looked in after supper, he pretended to be asleep. Early the next morning he left, avoiding Boris. In civilian clothes and a round hat, he wandered through the town, staring at the French and their uniforms and at the streets and buildings where the Russian and French Emperors were staying. In a square he saw tables being set up and preparations underway for the dinner; he saw Russian and French flags draped across the streets with huge monograms A and N. The windows of the houses also displayed flags and bunting.

"Boris doesn't want to help me, and I don't want to ask him. That's settled," Nicholas thought. "It's all over between us, but I won't leave without doing everything I can for Denisov — and certainly not without getting his letter to the Emperor. The Emperor! He's right here!" thought Rostov, who had unconsciously wandered back to the house where Alexander was staying.
Saddled horses stood before the building and the suite was assembling, evidently preparing for the Emperor to come out.

"I could see him at any moment," thought Rostov. "If only I could hand the letter to him directly and tell him everything... Would they really arrest me for being in civilian clothes? Surely not! He would understand who is in the right. He understands everything, knows everything. Who could be more just, more generous than he? And even if they did arrest me for being here — what would it matter?" he thought, looking at an officer entering the Emperor's residence. "People go in all the time. It's all nonsense! I'll go in and give the letter to the Emperor myself — so much the worse for Drubetskoy, who's driven me to it!" And with a resolve that surprised even himself, Rostov felt for the letter in his pocket and went straight to the house.

"No — I won't miss my chance this time, the way I did after Austerlitz," he thought, expecting at any moment to encounter the sovereign and feeling the blood rush to his heart at the thought. "I'll fall at his feet and beg him. He'll raise me up, listen, and even thank me. 'I am happy when I can do good, but to right an injustice is the greatest happiness,'" Rostov imagined the sovereign saying. And ignoring the curious stares of passersby, he entered the porch of the Emperor's residence.
A broad staircase led straight up from the entrance, and to the right he saw a closed door. Below, under the staircase, was a door to the lower floor.
"Whom do you want?" someone asked.
"To deliver a letter — a petition — to His Majesty," said Nicholas, his voice trembling.
"A petition? This way, to the officer on duty" — he was shown the door leading downstairs — "only it won't be accepted."

Hearing this indifferent voice, Rostov was struck with fear at what he was doing. The thought of encountering the Emperor at any moment was thrilling and therefore terrifying, and he was ready to bolt. But the official who had questioned him opened the door, and Rostov walked in.

A short, stocky man of about thirty, in white breeches, high boots, and a fine batiste shirt he had obviously just put on, stood in the room while his valet buttoned a new pair of handsome silk-embroidered suspenders onto the back of his breeches — which, for some reason, caught Rostov's attention. This man was speaking to someone in the next room.
"A good figure and in her first bloom," he was saying — but on seeing Rostov, he stopped and frowned.
"What is it? A petition?"
"What is it?" asked the person in the other room.
"Another petitioner," answered the man with the suspenders.
"Tell him to come back later. He'll be coming out soon — we need to go."
"Later... later! Tomorrow. It's too late..."
Rostov turned to leave, but the man in the suspenders stopped him.
"Who sent you? Who are you?"
"I come from Major Denisov," answered Rostov.
"Are you an officer?"
"Lieutenant Count Rostov."
"What nerve! Submit it through your commander. Now get along with you — go!" And he went back to putting on the uniform his valet was handing him.
Rostov went back into the hall and realized that the porch was now crowded with officers and generals in full dress uniform, through whom he had to pass.

Cursing his own audacity, his heart sinking at the thought of coming face to face with the Emperor and being humiliated and arrested in his presence — fully aware now of how improper his conduct was and regretting it — Rostov, with downcast eyes, was making his way out through the glittering suite when a familiar voice called him and a hand seized his arm.
"What are you doing here in civilian dress, sir?" asked a deep voice.
It was a cavalry general who had earned the Emperor's special favor during this campaign and who had previously commanded the division in which Rostov served.

Rostov began stammering an excuse, but seeing the general's kind, good-humored face, he pulled him aside and in an excited voice told him the whole story, begging him to intercede for Denisov, whom the general knew. After hearing him out, the general shook his head gravely.
"I'm sorry — sorry for the fine fellow. Give me the letter."

Barely had Rostov handed over the letter and finished explaining Denisov's case when hurried footsteps and the jingle of spurs were heard on the stairs, and the general, leaving him, went to the porch. The gentlemen of the Emperor's suite ran down the stairs to their horses. Hayne, the same groom who had been at Austerlitz, led up the Emperor's horse, and the faint creak of a footstep Rostov recognized at once sounded on the stairs. Forgetting the danger of being recognized, Rostov moved close to the porch with some curious civilians, and once again — after two years — he saw the features he adored: the same face, the same gaze, the same step, the same blend of majesty and gentleness. The feeling of enthusiasm and love for his sovereign rose again in Rostov's soul with all its old force. In his Preobrazhensky uniform — white leather breeches and high boots — wearing a star Rostov didn't recognize (it was the Legion of Honor), the sovereign came out onto the porch, pulling on his gloves and carrying his hat under his arm. He paused, looked around, and his glance seemed to brighten everything it touched. He spoke a few words to some generals, and recognizing the former commander of Rostov's division, smiled and beckoned him over.
The whole suite drew back, and Rostov saw the general talking with the Emperor for some time.

The Emperor said a few words and then stepped toward his horse. Again the crowd of courtiers and onlookers (Rostov among them) moved closer. Stopping beside his horse with one hand on the saddle, the Emperor turned to the cavalry general and said in a loud voice, clearly intending to be heard by all:
"I cannot do it, General. I cannot — because the law is stronger than I." And he put his foot in the stirrup.
The general bowed respectfully, and the sovereign mounted and rode off down the street at a gallop. Beside himself with emotion, Rostov ran after him with the crowd.
